justice: Both sides of the bridge provide sidewalks separated from motor traffic by solid railings, indicating basic space allocation for pedestrians alongside vehicles.
The carriageway is relatively narrow and constrained by rigid barriers, suggesting limited flexibility in reallocating space during congestion or incidents (potential equity concern among modes).

Physical separation elements (bridge parapets and metal fence) create a clear boundary, but there is no visible curb ramp/tactile guidance or marked accessible crossing points within the scene, limiting universal accessibility for all users in this segment.
safety: Mixed traffic is evident: a bus and cars share the motor lane while multiple e-scooters/motorbikes are riding very close to the curbside barrier, increasing side-swipe and merge conflict risk.
Rigid bridge barriers and fencing leave little recovery space/shoulder; if a vehicle or rider loses control, there is minimal lateral escape area.

Pedestrians are walking on the right-side sidewalk adjacent to fast-moving two-wheelers nearby, and there is no clearly marked protected cycle track; this proximity increases perceived and actual crash risk.
livability: The bridge environment is primarily traffic-oriented (bus, cars, and two-wheelers dominate the view), offering limited street-life functions beyond movement.
Some greenery and water-side trees are visible to the right beyond the railing, which can improve everyday experience, but the bridge segment itself has few social amenities.
No visible seating, pocket spaces, or active frontage on the bridge deck reduces opportunities for lingering and social interaction for all users.
sustainability: Presence of multiple two-wheelers suggests mode share beyond private cars, which can support lower-emission mobility if managed safely and efficiently.
A bus is present, indicating public transport use on this corridor, which generally supports more sustainable travel compared with single-occupancy vehicles.

Green vegetation along the right side (tree canopy beyond the bridge railing) contributes some ecological value, though the bridge deck itself shows little green infrastructure (no planters/permeable areas visible).
aesthetics: Consistent bridge railing design and repeating posts create visual rhythm and a coherent streetscape frame.
The view includes a substantial green tree line to the right and a relatively open skyline, improving scenic quality compared with fully built-up corridors.
However, prominent utility poles/overhead lines and a large communications tower dominate the skyline and reduce visual softness and harmony.
comfort: Thermal comfort is limited on the bridge deck: there is no visible shade structure or street trees on the bridge itself, and the open sky suggests high sun/wind exposure.
Physical comfort for pedestrians appears moderate: the sidewalk exists and is level, but it looks narrow and constrained by hard railings with no rest points (no benches) visible.
Psychological comfort is reduced by close-by traffic (bus, cars, and two-wheelers) and the confined corridor created by barriers, which can feel noisy and stressful for many users.
walkability: A continuous sidewalk is present on the right side, separated from motor lanes by railings/fencing, supporting basic pedestrian continuity along the bridge.
The walking space appears relatively narrow with hard edges (railing and fence), limiting comfortable passing and side-by-side walking, especially when pedestrians meet others.

Crossing opportunities and pedestrian priority features are not visible in this segment (no zebra markings/signals in view), which can reduce overall walk network permeability across directions on/near the bridge.
bikeability: No clearly marked or protected bike lane is visible; two-wheelers appear to operate in a narrow curbside space next to a metal fence, creating constrained operating width.
Potential conflicts are high due to mixing with heavier vehicles (bus and cars) in a tight bridge corridor, especially where lateral clearance is limited by rigid barriers.
No bicycle-specific wayfinding, markings, or bike parking facilities are visible, reducing cycling legibility and convenience for everyday riders.
